title: Controlling Gene Expression
summary: Learn how cells switch genes on and off through transcription factors and epigenetics.

lessons.title: Bacterial Operons: lac and trp

levels.kid:
Imagine a bacterium as a tiny kitchen. It only cooks what it needs. Why make a cake tool if there is no cake mix?

Bacteria keep related genes in a row, like recipe cards clipped together. This clipped set is called an **operon**. One switch turns the whole set on or off.

The **lac operon** makes tools to eat milk sugar, called lactose. When lactose shows up, the switch flips on. When it is gone, a guard protein sits on the switch and keeps it off.

The **trp operon** makes an amino acid called tryptophan. When the cell already has plenty, it stops making more. It's like not baking bread when the bread box is full. Smart, and it saves energy!
levels.hs:
Bacteria must save energy, so they make proteins only when needed. Many bacterial genes with related jobs sit side by side and are read together as one unit called an **operon**. An operon has:
- a **promoter**, where RNA polymerase (the enzyme that copies DNA into RNA) binds
- an **operator**, a short DNA "switch" next to the promoter
- several **structural genes**, all copied into one long mRNA

A **repressor** is a protein that binds the operator and blocks RNA polymerase.

**The lac operon** in *E. coli* holds genes for using lactose, including **lacZ** (beta-galactosidase, which splits lactose) and **lacY** (permease, which pumps lactose in). Normally the lac repressor sits on the operator, so the genes are off. When lactose is present, a form of it called **allolactose** binds the repressor and pulls it off the DNA. The genes turn on. This is an **inducible** operon.

**The trp operon** holds five genes for building the amino acid tryptophan. When tryptophan is scarce, the genes are on. When tryptophan is plentiful, it binds the trp repressor and helps it grab the operator, shutting the genes off. This is a **repressible** operon.

François Jacob and Jacques Monod worked out the lac operon in 1961 and shared the 1965 Nobel Prize.
levels.college:
An **operon** is a cluster of genes transcribed from one promoter into a single **polycistronic mRNA**, with one regulatory region controlling all of them.

**lac operon (inducible, catabolic)**
- Genes: **lacZ** (beta-galactosidase), **lacY** (lactose permease) and **lacA** (thiogalactoside transacetylase). The separate **lacI** gene makes the repressor from its own constitutive promoter.
- **Negative control:** the LacI tetramer binds the operator (lacO) and blocks transcription. The inducer **allolactose** binds LacI and causes an **allosteric** change that lowers its affinity for DNA. **IPTG** is a synthetic inducer that the cell does not break down.
- **Positive control:** when glucose is low, **cAMP** rises. cAMP binds **CAP** (also called CRP), and CAP-cAMP binds next to the promoter, helping recruit RNA polymerase. Strong expression needs lactose present **and** glucose absent.
- **Catabolite repression:** glucose transport lowers cAMP and also causes **inducer exclusion**, which blocks LacY. Both effects keep cells using glucose first. This produces **diauxic growth**: two growth phases with a lag between them.

**trp operon (repressible, biosynthetic)**
- Genes trpE, D, C, B, A encode the enzymes that build tryptophan.
- **Repression:** tryptophan acts as a **corepressor**. It binds the TrpR aporepressor, which then binds the operator.
- **Attenuation:** a leader region (**trpL**) contains two adjacent Trp codons and four segments that can pair (1 to 4). Translation and transcription are coupled. With plenty of Trp, the ribosome moves quickly over segment 1 and covers segment 2. Segments 3 and 4 then pair into a **terminator** hairpin, and transcription stops early. With little Trp, the ribosome stalls at the Trp codons. Segments 2 and 3 pair into an **antiterminator**, and transcription continues.

The two layers work at different scales. Repression changes expression about 70-fold, attenuation about 10-fold, and together they give roughly 700-fold control.
levels.phd:
**Genetic logic.** Jacob and Monod used **merodiploids** (F′ lac partial diploids) to separate *trans*-acting from *cis*-acting elements. Most **lacI⁻** mutations, which cause constitutive expression, were recessive: a wild-type lacI on the F′ restored control *in trans*. **Oᶜ** operator mutations were *cis*-dominant: they affected only genes on the same DNA molecule. Inducer-binding defects called **lacIˢ** (super-repressor) were dominant and made cells uninducible. Gilbert and Müller-Hill purified LacI in 1966 using radiolabeled IPTG binding. This was the first isolated repressor, and it confirmed that the repressor is a protein.

**DNA looping.** LacI is a dimer of dimers that binds the main operator **O1** and the auxiliary operators **O2** (in lacZ) and **O3** (upstream). Binding two operators at once loops the DNA between them, and the loop strengthens repression by about 50-fold or more (Oehler, Müller-Hill and colleagues). The crystal structure (Lewis et al., 1996) showed a helix-turn-helix headpiece that bends operator DNA. It also showed how IPTG binding moves the hinge helices and reduces the affinity for operator.

**CAP mechanism.** CAP-cAMP bends DNA by about 90° at a site centered near -61.5 in the lac promoter. Activating region 1 of CAP contacts the αCTD of RNA polymerase, an example of **Class I activation**. Glucose acts mainly through **EIIA^Glc** of the PTS sugar-uptake system. When unphosphorylated, EIIA^Glc inhibits LacY (inducer exclusion). Inducer exclusion probably contributes more to diauxie than falling cAMP does.

**Bistability.** Novick and Weiner (1957) showed all-or-none induction at low inducer concentrations. Positive feedback through permease (more LacY brings in more inducer) produces **hysteresis** in single cells (Ozbudak et al., 2004).

**trp attenuation** (Yanofsky). The model required tight coupling of translation and transcription. RNA polymerase pauses after the 1:2 hairpin forms, which lets the ribosome catch up. Attenuation responds to charged tRNA^Trp, not to free tryptophan. In *Bacillus subtilis*, the protein **TRAP** carries out an analogous control without a ribosome: Trp-bound TRAP binds the leader RNA and favors termination.
levels.expert:
**Why the operon still matters.** The lac system is the foundation of modern expression technology. **Blue-white screening** relies on α-complementation: an N-terminal lacZα fragment restores activity to the lacZΔM15 ω-fragment. A disrupted lacZα therefore gives white colonies on X-gal. The **T7 expression system** (BL21(DE3)) places T7 RNA polymerase under a lacUV5 promoter, and IPTG induces it. Practical pitfalls:
- **Leaky expression** of toxic proteins. Remedies include **lacIq** strains, the pLysS or pLysE plasmids (T7 lysozyme inhibits T7 RNA polymerase) and glucose in the medium.
- **Autoinduction:** lactose in complex media switches cells on as glucose runs out (Studier's autoinduction media).
- lacUV5 is less sensitive to CAP, so glucose suppresses it less than the wild-type promoter.

**Synthetic biology.** LacI, TetR and λ cI formed the **repressilator** (Elowitz and Leibler, 2000). LacI and cI repression also built the toggle switch (Gardner, Cantor and Collins, 2000). LacI/O variants are standard parts in genetic circuits and in mammalian inducible systems.

**Biophysics of search.** Single-molecule tracking in live *E. coli* (Hammar et al., 2012; Elf lab) showed LacI finding its operator by **facilitated diffusion**: it slides along about 45 bp of DNA per encounter, as predicted by Berg and von Hippel. Brief dissociation of LacI from its operator allows **stochastic bursts** of lac transcription. Choi et al. (2008) showed that rare complete dissociation from a DNA loop can trigger a phenotype switch.

**Beyond attenuation.** Trp-like leader peptides regulate many amino acid biosynthesis operons (his, leu, thr, pheA), and ribosome stalling is a recurring sensing strategy. Some antibiotic-resistance genes follow the same logic. For example, **ermC** is induced by translational attenuation when macrolides stall ribosomes on a leader peptide, exposing the ribosome-binding site. This matters clinically, because inducible erythromycin resistance can cause clindamycin failure (the D-test).

**Open questions:** how much the free energy of DNA looping depends on supercoiling and on nucleoid proteins (HU, IHF); how cells tune noise against response speed; and how evolution keeps operon gene order.

keyPoints: An operon is a cluster of genes transcribed together from one promoter
The lac operon is inducible: allolactose removes the LacI repressor
CAP-cAMP activates lac when glucose is low (catabolite repression)
The trp operon is repressible: tryptophan is a corepressor for TrpR
Attenuation uses ribosome stalling at Trp codons to choose terminator vs antiterminator
Jacob and Monod used cis/trans genetics to define operator and repressor

test.q: What is an operon?
choices: Genes transcribed together from one promoter
A protein that binds DNA in the nucleus
A single gene with several introns
test.explain: An operon is a gene cluster read into one polycistronic mRNA under shared control. Bacteria have no nucleus, and introns are not part of the definition.

test.q: What molecule acts as the natural inducer of the lac operon?
test.explain: Allolactose binds LacI and lowers its affinity for the operator. cAMP is an activator signal acting through CAP, not the inducer.

test.q: Under which condition is the lac operon expressed most strongly?
test.explain: The repressor must be removed (lactose present) and CAP-cAMP must be active (low glucose).

test.q: In the trp operon, what does tryptophan act as?
test.explain: Tryptophan binds the TrpR aporepressor so it can bind the operator and shut the operon off.

test.q: What does CAP-cAMP do at the lac promoter?
test.explain: CAP-cAMP is a positive regulator that binds near the promoter and recruits RNA polymerase when glucose is low.

test.q: Which gene encodes beta-galactosidase?
test.explain: lacZ encodes beta-galactosidase. lacY encodes permease and lacI encodes the repressor.

test.q: In trp attenuation, what happens when tryptophan is plentiful?
choices: The ribosome stalls on the leader
test.explain: A fast ribosome covers segment 2, so segments 3 and 4 pair into a terminator hairpin. Stalling happens when tryptophan is scarce.

test.q: The lac operon is best described as:
test.explain: It is switched on by its substrate to break down lactose. trp is the repressible, biosynthetic example.

test.q: Why is attenuation possible in bacteria?
choices: Their mRNA is spliced in the nucleus
test.explain: With no nucleus, ribosomes translate the leader while it is still being transcribed, so ribosome speed affects RNA folding.

test.q: What is the short DNA sequence called that the repressor binds?
test.explain: The operator lies next to the promoter. A bound repressor blocks transcription.

test.q: IPTG is a synthetic ___ of the lac operon that the cell does not break down.
test.explain: IPTG binds LacI like allolactose does but is not metabolized, which makes it useful in the lab.

test.q: Which two scientists proposed the operon model in 1961?
test.explain: François Jacob and Jacques Monod shared the 1965 Nobel Prize for this work.

kidTest.q: What is an operon?
choices: A kind of sugar found in milk
A tiny door in the cell wall
kidTest.explain: Genes clipped together share one on-off switch.

kidTest.q: What sugar does the lac operon help eat?
kidTest.explain: Lac stands for lactose, the sugar in milk.

kidTest.q: What keeps the lac genes off when there is no lactose?
choices: Extra glucose sugar in the cell
A thick fat layer around the gene
A guard protein on the switch
kidTest.explain: A repressor protein sits on the switch.

kidTest.q: When does the trp operon stop making tryptophan?
choices: When the cell temperature drops sharply
When lactose appears in the surroundings
kidTest.explain: Like not baking bread when the bread box is full.

kidTest.q: Bacteria make proteins only when needed to save e _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Making unneeded proteins wastes energy.

advancedTest.q: A merodiploid has an Oᶜ operator on the chromosome and a wild-type lac operon on an F′. Without inducer, what happens?
choices: F′ lacZ on, chromosomal lacZ off
Both copies are expressed equally well
Chromosomal lacZ on, F′ lacZ off
Neither copy of lacZ is expressed
advancedTest.explain: Oᶜ is cis-dominant. It affects only genes on its own DNA, while the wild-type F′ operator stays repressed.

advancedTest.q: Cells carry a lacIˢ mutation (repressor unable to bind inducer) plus a wild-type lacI on an F′. Expected phenotype?
advancedTest.explain: LacIˢ stays bound to the operator whatever the inducer level. Wild-type repressor cannot undo that, so lacIˢ is dominant.

advancedTest.q: Mutating both leader Trp codons to Ala codons would most likely make attenuation respond to:
advancedTest.explain: Attenuation senses whether the ribosome stalls at leader codons, which depends on the matching charged tRNA.

advancedTest.q: Why might diauxic lag persist in a mutant whose cAMP stays high even in glucose?
choices: CAP fails to bind DNA in that mutant
advancedTest.explain: Glucose uptake leaves EIIA^Glc unphosphorylated, and EIIA^Glc inhibits LacY. This keeps the inducer out even when cAMP is high.

lessons.title: Enhancers, Silencers and Transcription Factors

levels.kid:
Every cell in your body has the same instruction book, called DNA. But a brain cell and a muscle cell use different pages. How does each cell know which pages to read?

Special helper proteins called **transcription factors** decide. They grab onto little spots on the DNA, like sticky notes.

Some sticky notes say "Read this page loudly!" Those spots are called **enhancers**. Other sticky notes say "Skip this page!" Those are called **silencers**.

Here is the surprising part. An enhancer can sit far away from the page it controls. The DNA bends into a loop, like folding a long ribbon, so the far-away note can touch the right page.

This is how one instruction book can build many different kinds of cells.
levels.hs:
Your cells all carry the same genome, yet a neuron makes different proteins from a liver cell. The difference comes from **gene regulation**: controlling which genes are transcribed into RNA, and how much.

Key parts:
- The **promoter** is the DNA right at the start of a gene where **RNA polymerase II** assembles. On its own, it gives only a low, basal level of transcription.
- **Enhancers** are short DNA stretches that boost transcription. They can lie thousands of base pairs away, upstream, downstream, or even inside an intron, and they still work if flipped backward.
- **Silencers** are DNA stretches that reduce transcription.
- **Transcription factors** are proteins that recognize specific DNA sequences, usually 6 to 12 base pairs long. **Activators** bind enhancers; **repressors** bind silencers.

How does a distant enhancer reach its gene? The DNA forms a **loop** that brings the enhancer and promoter close together in 3D space.

A real example: the hemoglobin genes. A region called the **locus control region**, located far upstream of the beta-globin genes, acts like a master enhancer in red blood cell precursors. Through looping, it switches on the right globin gene at the right stage of development. That is why red blood cells make hemoglobin and skin cells do not.

Which genes a cell expresses depends on which transcription factors it contains.
levels.college:
Eukaryotic transcription by **RNA polymerase II** depends on combining several kinds of regulatory DNA with proteins that read it.

**Cis-regulatory elements** (on the same DNA molecule as the gene):
- **Core promoter**: elements such as the TATA box (about 25-30 bp upstream) and Inr. The **general transcription factors** (TFIID, which contains TBP, plus TFIIA, B, E, F and H) assemble here into the preinitiation complex.
- **Proximal promoter elements**: for example GC boxes bound by Sp1 and CAAT boxes bound by NF-Y.
- **Enhancers**: these work largely independent of distance and orientation, and are often 10-100+ kb away.
- **Silencers**: these recruit repressors.
- **Insulators**: these block an enhancer from acting on the wrong gene. In vertebrates they are usually bound by **CTCF**.

**Trans-acting factors** (proteins) are modular:
- A **DNA-binding domain (DBD)**. Classic families include C2H2 zinc fingers, homeodomains (helix-turn-helix), bZIP (e.g., AP-1 = Fos/Jun), bHLH (e.g., MyoD) and nuclear receptors.
- An **activation or repression domain**. Activation domains are often acidic and unstructured, as in VP16 or p53.

**Mechanisms of activation**:
- Activators recruit **coactivators**: the **Mediator** complex, which bridges to Pol II, and histone acetyltransferases such as **CBP/p300**.
- Enhancer-promoter **looping** is stabilized by Mediator, cohesin and other proteins.

**Mechanisms of repression**:
- Competing with activators for the same site, or masking an activation domain.
- Recruiting **corepressors** such as histone deacetylases (HDACs).

**Combinatorial control** means a small number of factors, used in different combinations, generates many cell-type-specific patterns. The **interferon-beta enhanceosome** is the textbook case: NF-kB, IRF3/7 and ATF-2/c-Jun bind cooperatively with HMG-I(Y). Only a complete assembly activates the gene.

Nuclear receptors show how signals reach DNA. The glucocorticoid receptor binds cortisol, moves into the nucleus and binds glucocorticoid response elements, turning hormone exposure into a transcriptional program.
levels.phd:
Enhancers were discovered in 1981, when Banerji, Rusconi and Schaffner showed that a 72-bp repeat from SV40 increased beta-globin reporter expression over 100-fold, independent of orientation and position. That operational definition still stands, but genomics has reshaped the concept.

**Identifying enhancers genome-wide.** ENCODE and Roadmap annotate putative enhancers by chromatin features:
- Open chromatin, detected by DNase-seq or ATAC-seq.
- H3K4me1 with **H3K27ac** for active enhancers; H3K4me1 with H3K27me3 for poised enhancers.
- Binding of p300.
- Bidirectional transcription of short, unstable **eRNAs**.

Current estimates run to hundreds of thousands of candidate elements in the human genome. **STARR-seq** and MPRAs test thousands of sequences functionally, but they assay activity outside the native chromosome.

**Grammar models.** Three models describe how motifs inside an enhancer are organized:
- **Enhanceosome**: strict arrangement and spacing of motifs (IFN-beta).
- **Billboard**: flexible arrangement of motifs.
- **TF collective**: requires the full set of factors, while individual motifs can be absent.

Most enhancers fall between these extremes. **Low-affinity sites** often confer specificity. Crocker and Stern showed that suboptimal Ubx/Exd sites in Drosophila *shavenbaby* enhancers prevent ectopic activation.

**Pioneer factors** such as FoxA and Sox2/Oct4 can bind DNA wrapped around nucleosomes and open closed chromatin. This underlies Yamanaka reprogramming with OSKM.

**3D topology.** Cohesin extrudes chromatin loops until it is halted by convergently oriented CTCF sites. This forms **TADs**, which constrain which promoters an enhancer can contact. Lupianez et al. (2015) showed that deleting or inverting TAD boundaries at *EPHA4* rewires enhancer contacts and causes limb malformations.

**Open debates.** How does looping produce transcription?
- Cohesin depletion abolishes most loops but alters relatively few genes acutely.
- Imaging at *Sox2* shows activation without close enhancer-promoter proximity.
- Alternatives include **phase-separated condensates**, formed by Mediator, BRD4 and intrinsically disordered activation domains, and "hub" models.

Transcription is **bursty**. Enhancers mainly raise **burst frequency**, while promoters influence burst size. Distinct **shadow enhancers** provide redundancy and robustness.
levels.expert:
Most disease-associated noncoding variation acts through enhancers. Roughly 90% of GWAS lead SNPs are noncoding, and they are enriched in cell-type-specific enhancers of the relevant tissue. Interpreting them is a central problem in translational genomics.

**Landmark clinical examples:**
- **ZRS**: a limb enhancer of *SHH*, located about 1 Mb away inside an intron of *LMBR1*. Single-base changes cause preaxial polydactyly. The distance between enhancer and gene foils naive "nearest gene" assignment.
- **BCL11A erythroid enhancer**: the basis of the first approved CRISPR therapy, exa-cel (Casgevy, approved 2023). Editing a GATA1 motif in this enhancer in patient stem cells lowers BCL11A only in the erythroid lineage. This de-represses fetal hemoglobin in sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia while sparing BCL11A function in other tissues.
- **FTO obesity locus**: the risk variant disrupts an ARID5B repressor site, increasing IRX3/IRX5 expression in adipocyte progenitors. The causal genes are not *FTO* itself.
- **Enhancer hijacking in cancer**: structural variants bring strong enhancers next to oncogenes. In medulloblastoma, GFI1/GFI1B are activated this way. In some IDH-mutant gliomas, hypermethylation of a CTCF site breaks an insulator, letting an enhancer drive *PDGFRA*. **Super-enhancers** (clusters of enhancers densely bound by Mediator and BRD4) at *MYC* create dependencies targeted by BET inhibitors and CDK7 inhibitors. Clinical efficacy of these drugs has been limited by toxicity.

**Drugging transcription factors.** TFs were long called "undruggable." Successes include:
- Ligand-binding domains of nuclear receptors (tamoxifen, enzalutamide).
- IMiDs (lenalidomide), which act as molecular glues directing cereblon to degrade IKZF1/3.
- Emerging PROTACs, including STAT3 degraders, and BCL6 degraders.

**Pitfalls for researchers:**
- Enhancer marks predict activity imperfectly.
- Reporter assays lack native chromatin.
- Assign targets with CRISPRi/CRISPRa perturbation screens (e.g., Fulco et al.'s CRISPRi-FlowFISH screens, which validated the ABC model), not by proximity alone.

**Open questions:** predicting enhancer activity from sequence (models such as Enformer and AlphaGenome remain imperfect at long range), and how enhancer-promoter specificity is encoded.

keyPoints: Transcription factors bind short specific DNA motifs to turn genes up or down
Enhancers boost transcription and work at a distance and in either orientation
Silencers recruit repressors; insulators bound by CTCF block wrong contacts
DNA looping, aided by Mediator and cohesin, brings enhancers to promoters
TFs are modular: a DNA-binding domain plus an activation or repression domain
Combinatorial control lets a few factors create many cell-type patterns

test.q: Which feature distinguishes an enhancer from a core promoter?
choices: It encodes the transcription factor protein
It is where RNA polymerase II first binds
It acts at a distance in either orientation
test.explain: Enhancers work largely independent of distance and orientation. The TATA box and polymerase assembly belong to the core promoter.

test.q: How does a distant enhancer contact its target promoter?
choices: The enhancer is copied next to the gene
The mRNA carries the enhancer to the gene
The DNA forms a loop in 3D space
The promoter slides along the chromosome
test.explain: Looping, stabilized by proteins such as Mediator and cohesin, brings the enhancer physically close to the promoter.

test.q: A transcription factor typically has which two functional parts?
choices: A catalytic site and a ribosome-binding site
A signal peptide and a transmembrane helix
A DNA-binding domain and an activation domain
An anticodon loop and an acceptor stem
test.explain: TFs are modular. One domain recognizes a DNA motif, and another activates or represses transcription by recruiting cofactors.

test.q: Which protein usually binds vertebrate insulators?
test.explain: CTCF binds insulator elements and, with cohesin, limits which promoters an enhancer can reach. TBP binds the TATA box.

test.q: Repressors bound at silencers often work by recruiting:
test.explain: Corepressors such as HDACs compact chromatin. Acetyltransferases like CBP/p300 are coactivators instead.

test.q: The Mediator complex mainly functions to:
choices: Add a cap to the new mRNA
Bridge activators to RNA polymerase II
Cut DNA at specific enhancer motifs
test.explain: Mediator is a coactivator that connects enhancer-bound activators to the polymerase machinery at the promoter.

test.q: The interferon-beta enhanceosome illustrates:
choices: Transcription by a single dominant factor
test.explain: NF-kB, IRFs and ATF-2/c-Jun bind cooperatively, and only the complete assembly activates the gene.

test.q: How does the glucocorticoid receptor change gene expression?
choices: It binds cortisol, enters the nucleus and binds DNA
It opens ion channels that alter transcription
It degrades mRNAs that carry response elements
It phosphorylates RNA polymerase in the cytoplasm
test.explain: This nuclear receptor binds its hormone, moves into the nucleus and binds glucocorticoid response elements.

test.q: The beta-globin locus control region is an example of:
choices: A silencer active in skin cells
test.explain: The LCR sits far upstream and, through looping, drives globin expression in red blood cell precursors.

test.q: Which enzyme transcribes protein-coding genes in eukaryotes? (two words or with numeral)
test.explain: RNA polymerase II assembles at the promoter with the general transcription factors.

test.q: DNA stretches that reduce transcription by recruiting repressors are called ___.
test.explain: Silencers are the counterpart of enhancers. Repressors bind them to lower expression.

test.q: The TATA box is bound by the TATA-binding protein, part of the general factor TFII___.
test.explain: TFIID contains TBP and starts assembly of the preinitiation complex.

kidTest.q: What do transcription factors do?
choices: Help choose which genes get read
Break food down in the stomach
kidTest.explain: They stick to DNA and decide which pages of the instruction book are used.

kidTest.q: What does an enhancer tell the cell?
kidTest.explain: Enhancers turn genes up.

kidTest.q: What does a silencer tell the cell?
kidTest.explain: Silencers turn genes down.

kidTest.q: How can a far-away enhancer reach its page?
choices: The DNA bends into a loop
The page tears off and moves
kidTest.explain: The DNA folds like a ribbon so the two spots touch.

kidTest.q: The instruction book in every cell is called D _ _.
kidTest.explain: DNA holds the instructions, and cells use different parts of it.

advancedTest.q: Acute cohesin depletion abolishes most chromatin loops yet changes relatively few genes. What does this most directly suggest?
choices: Promoters can drive high output without any factors
CTCF by itself mediates enhancer-promoter contact
Ongoing activation may persist without stable loops
Most enhancers are nonfunctional sequences in vivo
advancedTest.explain: The mismatch suggests established activation can persist without loops, which supports condensate or hub models alongside looping.

advancedTest.q: Why does editing the BCL11A erythroid enhancer beat knocking out the BCL11A gene for sickle cell therapy?
choices: It inserts an extra fetal globin gene into stem cells
It raises BCL11A levels across many different tissues
It lowers BCL11A in red cell precursors, sparing others
It directly repairs the sickle mutation in beta-globin
advancedTest.explain: Enhancers are lineage-specific, so disrupting this one de-represses fetal hemoglobin without losing BCL11A function elsewhere.

advancedTest.q: Suboptimal Ubx/Exd sites in shavenbaby enhancers imply that low-affinity sites:
choices: Help keep enhancer activity restricted to the right cells
Turn enhancers into insulators bound by CTCF
Are evolutionary errors that weaken enhancer function
Raise burst size by strengthening the promoter
advancedTest.explain: Raising affinity caused ectopic activation, so weak sites encode specificity rather than defects.

advancedTest.q: A GWAS SNP lies in an intron of gene A, 1 Mb from gene B. What is the best way to assign its target gene?
choices: Choose whichever gene has the strongest promoter
Use CRISPRi perturbation of the element and measure effects
Assume gene A because it is the nearest gene
Pick the gene with the most exons in the TAD
advancedTest.explain: Cases like ZRS/SHH and FTO/IRX3 show proximity misleads. Functional perturbation establishes the true target gene.

lessons.title: DNA Methylation, CpG Islands and Imprinting

levels.kid:
Your DNA is like a giant cookbook with thousands of recipes, called genes. Every cell has the same book. But a skin cell and a brain cell don't cook the same recipes!

How does a cell know which recipes to skip? It sticks tiny tags on some pages. These tags are called **methyl groups**. A page covered in tags is hard to read, so that gene stays quiet. The words on the page don't change. Only the tags do.

Here is a cool twist. You get one cookbook from Mom and one from Dad. For a few special recipes, the cell only reads Mom's copy or only Dad's copy. The other copy is tagged shut. This is called **imprinting**. It is like each parent leaving sticky notes on their book.
levels.hs:
**DNA methylation** is the addition of a small chemical group, a methyl group (CH3), to DNA. In humans it almost always happens on the base **cytosine** when cytosine is followed by guanine. This two-letter pattern is written **CpG** (the "p" is the phosphate linking them).

Methylation doesn't change the DNA sequence, so it is called **epigenetic**: a heritable change in gene activity without a change in the letters. When a gene's promoter (its "on switch" region) is heavily methylated, the gene is usually turned off.

Key ideas:
- About 70-80% of CpGs in the human genome are methylated.
- **CpG islands** are stretches, often around 1,000 base pairs long, packed with CpGs. Many sit at gene promoters and usually stay *unmethylated*, keeping those genes ready to use.
- Enzymes called **DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs)** add methyl groups. When a cell divides, DNMT1 copies the pattern onto the new DNA strand, so daughter cells "remember" which genes are off.

**Genomic imprinting** is a special case. For about 100-200 human genes, only the copy from one parent is active, because the other copy was methylated in the egg or sperm. A real example: **Prader-Willi syndrome** happens when the father's copy of a region on chromosome 15 is lost. The mother's copy is imprinted (silenced), so the needed genes aren't expressed.
levels.college:
In mammals, DNA methylation means **5-methylcytosine (5mC)**, made mostly at CpG dinucleotides. Because CpG is palindromic, methylation is usually symmetric on both strands, which lets it be copied.

**The enzymes**
- **DNMT3A and DNMT3B**: *de novo* methyltransferases that set new patterns, especially in early embryos and germ cells. DNMT3L is a catalytically inactive partner that boosts their activity.
- **DNMT1**: the *maintenance* methyltransferase. Its partner **UHRF1** recognizes hemimethylated CpGs just behind the replication fork, and DNMT1 methylates the new strand.
- All use **S-adenosylmethionine (SAM)** as the methyl donor.
- **TET enzymes** (TET1-3) oxidize 5mC to 5hmC, 5fC and 5caC. 5fC and 5caC can be removed by thymine DNA glycosylase plus base excision repair, giving *active demethylation*. Failure of DNMT1 maintenance during division gives *passive demethylation*.

**CpG depletion and islands.** The genome has only about a quarter of the expected CpGs. Methylated cytosine tends to deaminate into thymine, a mutation that is poorly repaired, so CpGs have eroded over evolution. **CpG islands** escaped this because they stay unmethylated in the germline. About 60-70% of human gene promoters, including most housekeeping genes, contain one.

**How methylation silences genes**
- It directly blocks binding of some transcription factors, such as CTCF.
- **Methyl-CpG-binding domain proteins** (MeCP2, MBD1-4) read 5mC and recruit repressive complexes that compact chromatin.

**Imprinting.** Imprints are set in the germline at **imprinting control regions (ICRs)** and survive the genome-wide erasure after fertilization. At the **H19/IGF2** locus, the maternal ICR is unmethylated, so CTCF binds and insulates IGF2 from shared enhancers; H19 is expressed. On the paternal allele the ICR is methylated, CTCF can't bind, and IGF2 is expressed. Disorders include Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes (15q11-q13), and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (11p15).
levels.phd:
Mammalian methylation landscapes are bimodal: most CpGs are about 70-80% methylated, while CpG islands (CGIs) are largely unmethylated. Gardiner-Garden and Frommer defined CGIs empirically: over 200 bp, GC content above 50%, and an observed/expected CpG ratio above 0.6. Later definitions such as Takai-Jones tightened these thresholds to exclude Alu repeats. CGI protection is active. The CXXC-domain proteins (CFP1, KDM2A/B, TET1) bind unmethylated CpG, and promoter-associated H3K4me3 inhibits DNMT3 recruitment, because the DNMT3 ADD domain binds only unmodified H3K4. By contrast, the DNMT3B PWWP domain reads H3K36me3, explaining high methylation in transcribed gene bodies.

Maintenance is less faithful than the semiconservative model of Holliday-Pugh and Riggs (1975) implied. DNMT1 has measurable error rates, and de novo activity contributes continuously. This supports a dynamic, stochastic equilibrium in which some UHRF1 mechanisms involve ubiquitinated H3 (H3K18/K23ub) recruiting DNMT1. Mouse knockouts are telling: loss of Dnmt1 or Dnmt3b is embryonic lethal, and Dnmt3a nulls die a few weeks after birth.

The causality debate persists: is methylation a cause of silencing or a lock after silencing? At CGI promoters it typically follows Polycomb or other repression, stabilizing long-term states such as X inactivation and germline gene silencing. Non-CpG (CpH) methylation accumulates in neurons and is read by MeCP2. Loss-of-function MECP2 mutations cause Rett syndrome.

Reprogramming happens twice. After fertilization, the paternal pronucleus undergoes TET3-dependent oxidation, while the maternal genome loses methylation more passively. In primordial germ cells, near-complete erasure, including imprints, precedes sex-specific re-establishment. ICRs escape the post-zygotic wave through **ZFP57/KAP1(TRIM28)**, which binds methylated TGCCGC hexamers and recruits SETDB1 and DNMTs. Most germline differentially methylated regions are maternal, set by DNMT3A/3L during oocyte growth, often depending on transcription through the locus. Only a few (H19, Dlk1-Meg3/IG-DMR, Rasgrf1) are paternal. The parental conflict (kinship) hypothesis of Haig explains why growth-promoting genes (IGF2) tend to be paternally expressed and growth restrictors (IGF2R, CDKN1C) maternally expressed. This is supported but contested, and imprinted gene functions in brain and behaviour complicate a purely growth-centred view.
levels.expert:
Clinically, methylation is both a biomarker and a drug target. In cancer the pattern is paradoxical: global hypomethylation, which promotes genomic instability and repeat activation, occurs alongside focal CGI hypermethylation silencing tumour suppressors (CDKN2A, MLH1, BRCA1). **CIMP** (CpG island methylator phenotype) defines subsets of colorectal cancer and glioma. In gliomas, IDH1/2 mutations produce 2-hydroxyglutarate, which inhibits TET enzymes and drives G-CIMP. IDH-mutant tumours have markedly better prognosis. **MGMT promoter methylation** in glioblastoma predicts benefit from temozolomide: silencing the repair enzyme leaves O6-methylguanine lesions unrepaired. This is routinely assayed by methylation-specific PCR or pyrosequencing, though cut-offs remain inconsistent between labs.

For a future neurosurgeon, the most consequential advance is **methylation-based CNS tumour classification**. Capper et al. (Nature 2018) used array profiles from about 2,800 tumours to train a random-forest classifier. It revised the diagnosis in roughly 12% of cases, and methylation classes are now integrated into WHO CNS5 (2021). Pitfalls include low tumour purity, "no match" calibration scores, and classes defined only by methylation. Rapid nanopore sequencing now enables near-intraoperative classification.

Pharmacology: the nucleoside analogues **azacitidine** and **decitabine** incorporate into DNA and covalently trap DNMTs, causing their degradation. They are approved for myelodysplastic syndromes and AML. Their effect is replication-dependent and slow, and response correlates poorly with demethylation of specific genes. Viral mimicry, in which reactivated endogenous retroviruses trigger dsRNA sensing and interferon responses, may contribute. Folate and SAM metabolism link nutrition to methylation, although human evidence is weaker than in agouti mouse models.

Methods: bisulfite converts unmethylated C to U but cannot distinguish 5mC from 5hmC. Oxidative bisulfite, TAPS and enzymatic (EM-seq) approaches resolve this or reduce DNA damage. Long-read sequencing reads modifications directly with haplotype phasing, which is ideal for imprinting. Imprinting diagnostics must account for distinct mechanisms: deletions, uniparental disomy, epimutations and multilocus imprinting disturbance. Assisted reproduction is associated with a small increased risk of Beckwith-Wiedemann and Angelman epimutations. Epigenetic clocks (Horvath) estimate biological age, but whether clock CpGs are causal remains open.

Under study: dCas9-DNMT3A/TET1 epi-editing to silence or reactivate genes durably without cutting DNA.

keyPoints: DNA methylation adds a methyl group to cytosine, mainly at CpG sites
Promoter methylation usually silences genes without changing the sequence
DNMT3A/3B set new patterns; DNMT1 with UHRF1 maintains them after replication
CpG islands at many promoters normally stay unmethylated
TET enzymes oxidize 5mC as a route to active demethylation
Imprinting: parent-specific methylation at control regions silences one allele

lessons.title: Histone Modifications and Chromatin Remodeling

levels.kid:
Your DNA is super long. To fit inside a tiny cell, it wraps around little balls of protein called **histones**, like thread wound around spools.

When the thread is wound up tight, the cell can't read the genes there. When it is loose, the cell can read them and make what it needs.

Cells stick tiny tags onto the histones. Some tags mean "loosen up, read me!" Other tags mean "stay tight, keep this closed!"

There are also helper machines that push and slide the spools along the thread. That opens up spots that need to be read.

This is how a brain cell and a skin cell can have the same DNA but do different jobs. They open different pages of the same book.
levels.hs:
Each human cell holds about 2 meters of DNA. It is packed into a nucleus only a few micrometers wide. The basic packing unit is the **nucleosome**: about 147 base pairs of DNA wrapped around a core of eight **histone** proteins. These are two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4. DNA plus its proteins is called **chromatin**.

Chromatin comes in two broad states:
- **Euchromatin**: loosely packed and accessible, with active genes.
- **Heterochromatin**: tightly packed, with mostly silent genes.

Histones have floppy "tails" that stick out of the nucleosome. Enzymes add chemical groups to these tails, which are called **histone modifications**. **Acetylation** adds an acetyl group to the amino acid lysine. This removes lysine's positive charge, so the histone grips the negatively charged DNA less tightly, and genes tend to switch on. **Methylation** can mean on or off, depending on which lysine carries it.

Separately, **chromatin remodeling complexes** use energy from ATP to slide, eject or swap nucleosomes. This exposes DNA to transcription factors.

A real example: the drug **vorinostat** blocks histone deacetylases (HDACs), the enzymes that remove acetyl groups. It is approved to treat a type of lymphoma (cutaneous T-cell lymphoma), partly by reactivating silenced genes.
levels.college:
Chromatin structure is a major control point for transcription. Histone N-terminal tails are heavily modified, and these marks change both the physical properties of chromatin and which proteins bind it.

**Acetylation.** **Histone acetyltransferases (HATs)**, such as p300/CBP and GCN5, transfer acetyl groups from acetyl-CoA to lysines. This neutralizes the lysines' positive charge and weakens histone-DNA and nucleosome-nucleosome contacts. **Bromodomain** proteins read acetyl-lysine. **HDACs** reverse the mark and are often recruited by repressors.

**Methylation.** **Histone methyltransferases** use S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) to add one, two or three methyl groups to lysines, or methyl groups to arginines. Methylation does not change charge, so its effect depends on the proteins that read it:
- **H3K4me3**: found at active promoters.
- **H3K36me3**: found across actively transcribed gene bodies.
- **H3K27ac** plus **H3K4me1**: active enhancers.
- **H3K9me3**: constitutive heterochromatin, read by HP1's **chromodomain**.
- **H3K27me3**: deposited by **Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2)**, whose catalytic subunit is EZH2. It silences developmental genes.

Demethylases reverse methyl marks. These include LSD1 (a FAD-dependent enzyme) and the JmjC family (which need Fe(II) and α-ketoglutarate).

**Other marks** include phosphorylation (H3S10ph during mitosis), ubiquitination (H2AK119ub by PRC1, H2BK120ub linked to transcription) and histone variants such as **H2A.Z** at promoters and **CENP-A** at centromeres.

**ATP-dependent remodelers** come in four families:
- **SWI/SNF**: slides and ejects nucleosomes to open promoters.
- **ISWI**: spaces nucleosomes evenly.
- **CHD**: varied roles, including the NuRD complex, which also contains HDACs.
- **INO80/SWR1**: exchanges H2A for H2A.Z.

The **writer/reader/eraser** framework summarizes the system. Writers add marks, readers interpret them, and erasers remove them, turning chromatin into a dynamic signaling surface.
levels.phd:
Allis and Strahl proposed the **histone code hypothesis** in 2000. It held that combinations of modifications specify downstream outcomes. Two ideas from it still hold up: marks recruit effector proteins, and marks cross-talk with each other. One example of cross-talk is that H2BK120 ubiquitination by RNF20/40 is required for Dot1L to make H3K79 methylation and for COMPASS to make H3K4 trimethylation. Another is the methyl/phos switch: H3S10 phosphorylation ejects HP1 from H3K9me3 during mitosis. However, a strictly combinatorial "code" has been criticized. Many marks correlate with transcription rather than cause it, and some are a consequence of polymerase passage. For example, Set2 travels with Ser2-phosphorylated Pol II to deposit H3K36me3, which recruits Rpd3S deacetylase to suppress cryptic intragenic initiation.

Mechanistically, Allfrey (1964) linked acetylation to RNA synthesis. Brownell and Allis (1996) identified Tetrahymena p55, a homolog of yeast Gcn5, as the first nuclear HAT. Shogren-Knaak et al. (2006) showed that H4K16ac alone blocks 30-nm fiber compaction in vitro, a direct structural effect. In contrast, most methyl marks act through reader domains such as chromo, PHD, Tudor, PWWP and BAH. Aromatic cages in these domains discriminate methylation state and surrounding sequence.

Heritability is the key question for calling a mark "epigenetic." H3K27me3 propagates by a read-write loop. EED, a PRC2 subunit, binds existing H3K27me3 and allosterically stimulates EZH2. This lets PRC2 restore the mark on newly deposited histones after replication. H3K9me3 uses a similar loop: Clr4/SUV39H's chromodomain recognizes the methyl mark that the enzyme itself deposits. Tethering experiments in fission yeast (Audergon, Ragunathan, 2015) showed that H3K9 methylation can be inherited for many generations after the initiator is removed, but only when the eraser Epe1 is absent.

Remodelers use translocase domains of the SF2 helicase family. These pump DNA through the nucleosome at superhelical location 2. Biochemical and cryo-EM studies of ISWI (Snf2h) bound to nucleosomes reveal how ISWI is autoinhibited until it senses the H4 tail basic patch and linker DNA length. This explains how ISWI produces regular spacing.

Chromatin marks are also coupled to metabolism. Acetylation depends on acetyl-CoA levels, and methylation depends on SAM. Demethylation by JmjC enzymes needs α-KG and is inhibited by 2-hydroxyglutarate.
levels.expert:
Chromatin regulators are among the most frequently mutated genes in cancer. About 20% of human tumors carry mutations in SWI/SNF (BAF) subunits. **SMARCB1** loss defines malignant rhabdoid and atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumors (AT/RT). These are aggressive pediatric CNS tumors with otherwise very quiet genomes. Loss of SMARCB1 removes BAF's opposition to PRC2, which creates a dependency on EZH2. That dependency is the rationale for **tazemetostat**, an EZH2 inhibitor. It is FDA-approved for epithelioid sarcoma (also SMARCB1-deficient) and for EZH2-mutant or refractory follicular lymphoma.

The **oncohistones** matter directly to a future neurosurgeon. **H3K27M**, a lysine-to-methionine substitution usually in H3F3A (H3.3) or HIST1H3B, defines **diffuse midline glioma, H3 K27-altered**. This is a WHO CNS5 entity that includes most diffuse intrinsic pontine gliomas (DIPG). The mutant tail inhibits PRC2 dominantly, causing global loss of H3K27me3, although some loci keep it. **H3.3 G34R/V** marks hemispheric gliomas in adolescents, and H3K36M occurs in chondroblastoma. Immunohistochemistry for H3K27M and for H3K27me3 loss is now routine in neuropathology. **ONC201 (dordaviprone)**, which acts on DRD2 and ClpP rather than on chromatin, received accelerated FDA approval in 2025 for H3K27M-mutant diffuse midline glioma. Biopsy approaches to the brainstem now matter for trial eligibility.

Other drug classes:
- **HDAC inhibitors**: vorinostat, romidepsin and panobinostat. They have modest selectivity, cause thrombocytopenia and fatigue, and some carry QT effects.
- **BET bromodomain inhibitors**: JQ1 is the tool compound. Trials have been limited by toxicity and modest single-agent activity.
- **Menin inhibitors** such as revumenib (approved 2024) block the menin–KMT2A interaction in KMT2A-rearranged leukemia. **DOT1L** inhibition has been explored for the same disease.

Methodological pitfalls:
- **Antibody specificity.** ChIP-seq relies on antibodies that may cross-react between methylation states. Spike-in normalization is needed when global mark levels change, as in H3K27M cells.
- **CUT&RUN/CUT&Tag.** These lower cell-input requirements, enabling clinical samples and single-cell work.
- **Correlation versus causation.** dCas9 fused to p300 or KRAB/DNMT3 can test causation at individual loci. Notably, Drosophila histone H3K4R mutants (Hödl and Basler) still transcribe many genes.

Key open questions include how much transcriptional memory histone marks truly encode, and how phase separation by HP1 and Polycomb proteins contributes to chromatin compartments.

Lysine acetylation neutralizes charge and generally opens chromatin
Histone methylation is context-specific: H3K4me3 marks active promoters; H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 mark repression
Writers, readers (bromo-, chromodomains) and erasers (HDACs, demethylases) control marks
ATP-dependent remodelers (SWI/SNF, ISWI, CHD, INO80) slide, evict or swap nucleosomes
Chromatin regulator mutations drive cancers like H3K27M diffuse midline glioma

lessons.title: Regulatory RNAs: miRNA, siRNA and lncRNA

levels.kid:
Your cells make little messages called RNA. Most of them are recipes the cell uses to build proteins. But some RNAs are not recipes at all. They are bosses that help decide which recipes get used.

Some bosses are tiny. A **microRNA** is like a sticky note that grabs a recipe and says, "Not today!" Then the recipe gets used less or thrown away.

Other bosses are very long. A **long noncoding RNA** can work like a big flag that tells helper proteins where to go. One famous long RNA, called Xist, covers a whole extra X chromosome in girls and makes it go quiet.

So RNA is not just a messenger. Sometimes it is the one giving orders!
levels.hs:
Most genes are copied into messenger RNA (mRNA), which ribosomes read to build proteins. But a large share of the RNA a cell makes never codes for protein. Many of these **noncoding RNAs** help control which genes are active. Three big groups matter here:

- **MicroRNAs (miRNAs)**: about 22 nucleotides long, made from the cell's own genes. A miRNA pairs with a matching stretch of an mRNA, usually in its 3' untranslated region (3' UTR). That makes the mRNA be translated less and often broken down faster. One miRNA can tune hundreds of genes a little.
- **Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs)**: also about 21-23 nucleotides, usually made from long double-stranded RNA, such as viral RNA or RNA added in the lab. siRNAs match their target perfectly and cause it to be cut. This is called **RNA interference (RNAi)**.
- **Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs)**: longer than 200 nucleotides. They often act as scaffolds or guides that bring proteins to particular places on DNA.

A real example: the first miRNA, **lin-4**, was found in 1993 in the worm *C. elegans* by Victor Ambros's lab, working alongside Gary Ruvkun. lin-4 turns down the gene lin-14 so the worm moves on to its next stage of development. Ambros and Ruvkun won the 2024 Nobel Prize for this discovery. Andrew Fire and Craig Mello had won the 2006 prize for discovering RNAi.
levels.college:
**miRNA biogenesis.** RNA polymerase II transcribes a primary miRNA (**pri-miRNA**) that contains a hairpin. In the nucleus, the **Microprocessor** complex (the RNase III enzyme **Drosha** plus its partner **DGCR8**) crops out a hairpin of about 70 nucleotides, the **pre-miRNA**. **Exportin-5** carries it to the cytoplasm. There **Dicer** cuts off the loop, leaving a duplex of about 22 base pairs. One strand, the guide, is loaded into an **Argonaute (AGO)** protein to form the **RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC)**. The other strand, the passenger, is thrown away.

**Target recognition.** In animals, the miRNA mostly pairs through its **seed region** (nucleotides 2-8) with sites in the 3' UTR. Because pairing is only partial, AGO does not cut the target. Instead it recruits **GW182/TNRC6**, which brings in the CCR4-NOT deadenylase. The poly(A) tail is shortened, the mRNA is decapped and degraded, and translation is repressed. Plant miRNAs often pair almost perfectly and lead to cleavage.

**siRNA pathway.** Long double-stranded RNA, or a short hairpin RNA (shRNA), is processed by Dicer into siRNAs. With full complementarity, **AGO2** cuts the target between nucleotides 10 and 11 of the guide. This is slicing, and it gives strong, specific knockdown. RNAi is a key antiviral defense in plants and invertebrates, and a standard lab tool.

**lncRNAs** act by several mechanisms:
- **Guide/scaffold**: **Xist** coats one X chromosome in female mammals and recruits silencers such as SPEN and PRC2, so that X chromosome is inactivated.
- **cis-acting**: the act of transcribing a lncRNA, or the RNA itself, regulates nearby genes, as in imprinted clusters (Airn, Kcnq1ot1).
- **Decoy/sponge**: some RNAs bind miRNAs or proteins and keep them away from their targets.
- **trans-acting**: **HOTAIR** has been reported to help direct PRC2 and LSD1 to distant genes.

**piRNAs**, a fourth class, partner with PIWI proteins to silence transposons in the germline.
levels.phd:
**Quantitative targeting.** Seed pairing hierarchy: 8mer (seed plus an A opposite position 1) > 7mer-m8 > 7mer-A1 > 6mer. Context features also improve repression: AU-rich surroundings, sites positioned away from the stop codon, and 3' supplementary pairing at nucleotides 13-16. TargetScan (Bartel lab) models these features. Typical repression of a single target is modest, often less than twofold. Ribosome profiling (Guo et al., 2010) showed that at steady state, most of the repression is explained by mRNA decay rather than translational block. Translational repression comes earlier in time but is quantitatively smaller. More than 60% of human protein-coding genes contain conserved miRNA sites under selection (Friedman et al., 2009).

**Strand selection and AGO.** The guide strand tends to be the one whose 5' end sits at the less stably paired end of the duplex (thermodynamic asymmetry). A 5' U or A also helps, because the AGO MID domain prefers them. Humans have four AGO proteins. Only AGO2 slices efficiently, and slicing also requires near-complete pairing across the central region. Target-directed miRNA degradation (TDMD) is the reverse case: extensive pairing at the 3' end recruits the ZSWIM8 ubiquitin ligase, which marks AGO for destruction, so the exposed miRNA is degraded.

**The ceRNA controversy.** The competing-endogenous-RNA hypothesis (Salmena et al., 2011) proposed that transcripts "sponge" shared miRNAs and so regulate one another. Stoichiometric studies (Denzler et al., 2014; Bosson et al., 2014) argued that physiological changes in a single transcript rarely change total site abundance enough to matter. Effective sponging needs huge numbers of sites, as in the circular RNA **CDR1as/ciRS-7**, which carries about 70 miR-7 sites.

**lncRNA rigor.** Many lncRNAs are poorly conserved and present at fewer than one copy per cell. Their claimed functions often fail to separate three possibilities: the RNA product itself, the act of transcription, or the DNA element at the locus. To tell these apart, researchers compare knockdowns (ASO, CRISPRi) with promoter deletion, insertion of a poly(A) signal that stops transcription early, and rescue from another chromosomal location. Strong examples include Xist, whose A-repeat binds SPEN and is needed for silencing, and the **Kcnq1ot1/Airn** imprinted loci. In Airn, overlap by transcription, not the RNA sequence, silences Igf2r (Latos et al., 2012). HOTAIR's trans function has been disputed: the mouse knockout phenotype was mild, and PRC2 binds RNA without much specificity.
levels.expert:
**Therapeutic siRNAs.** RNAi has become a drug platform. **Patisiran** (2018, lipid nanoparticle) was the first approved siRNA, followed by GalNAc conjugates that bind the hepatocyte asialoglycoprotein receptor: givosiran (acute hepatic porphyria), lumasiran (primary hyperoxaluria type 1), **inclisiran** (PCSK9, dosed only a few times a year) and vutrisiran (hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis). Chemical modification makes this durability possible: 2'-O-methyl and 2'-fluoro sugars plus phosphorothioate linkages resist nucleases and reduce innate immune sensing through TLR7/8. Delivery outside the liver is the frontier. Lipophilic (C16) conjugates are reaching the CNS, with ALN-APP lowering amyloid precursor protein after intrathecal delivery. This is directly relevant to neurology and neurosurgery.

**Pitfalls in RNAi experiments.** An siRNA can act like a miRNA: its seed sequence represses hundreds of unintended transcripts. Many early genome-wide screen hits were later traced to this seed effect. Good practice uses multiple independent siRNAs, rescue with a cDNA resistant to the siRNA, and seed-matched controls. Results should then be confirmed with CRISPR knockout, keeping in mind that genetic compensation can hide phenotypes in knockouts.

**miRNAs as drugs and biomarkers.** Anti-miR therapy (miravirsen against miR-122 in hepatitis C) proved the concept, but miRNA mimics have struggled. MRX34, a miR-34a mimic, was halted after severe immune-related adverse events. Circulating miRNAs are appealing biomarkers, but signals from hemolysis (miR-451, miR-16), platelet contamination and normalization choices distort many studies. In neuro-oncology, miR-10b in glioblastoma and miRNA cargo in extracellular vesicles remain investigational.

**Neurobiology.** Neurons rely heavily on local regulation. Mice lacking Dicer in specific neuron types show neurodegeneration. miR-134 regulates dendritic spine size, and miR-9/miR-124 drive neuronal fate. Among lncRNAs, **Malat1** is abundant in neurons, yet its knockout mice are viable. That result shows abundance does not equal essentiality.

**Open questions.**
- What fraction of the roughly 20,000 annotated human lncRNAs function as RNA molecules?
- Do micropeptides encoded by "noncoding" RNAs explain some reported functions?
- How do RNA-binding phase condensates, such as paraspeckles scaffolded by NEAT1, contribute to gene regulation?

keyPoints: Many RNAs regulate genes without coding for protein
miRNAs (~22 nt) are made by Drosha, then Dicer, and loaded into Argonaute (RISC)
Animal miRNAs pair via the seed (nt 2-8), mostly in 3' UTRs, causing decay and translational repression
siRNAs pair perfectly and direct AGO2 to slice the target (RNAi)
lncRNAs (>200 nt) act as guides, scaffolds and decoys, e.g., Xist in X inactivation
GalNAc-siRNA drugs such as inclisiran bring RNAi to the clinic

test.q: Which enzyme cuts the pre-miRNA hairpin in the cytoplasm to produce a short duplex?
test.explain: Dicer removes the loop in the cytoplasm. Drosha, with DGCR8, acts earlier, in the nucleus.

test.q: Animal miRNAs mainly recognize targets through pairing of which region?
test.explain: Seed pairing (nucleotides 2-8) is the main determinant of target recognition in animals.

test.q: Where in an mRNA are animal miRNA binding sites most commonly found?
test.explain: Most functional animal miRNA sites lie in the 3' untranslated region.

test.q: How does an siRNA usually silence its target compared with an animal miRNA?
test.explain: With full complementarity, AGO2 cleaves the target mRNA. Partial pairing by animal miRNAs instead causes decay and translational repression.

test.q: Which lncRNA coats one X chromosome to inactivate it in female mammals?
test.explain: Xist spreads along one X chromosome and recruits silencing proteins such as SPEN and PRC2.

test.q: The first miRNA discovered, lin-4, regulates which target in C. elegans?
test.explain: lin-4 represses lin-14, which allows developmental timing to progress.

test.q: What is the main repressive outcome when GW182 recruits CCR4-NOT to an mRNA?
test.explain: CCR4-NOT deadenylates the mRNA, which leads to decapping and decay.

test.q: The RNA-induced silencing complex is built around which protein family?
test.explain: The guide strand is loaded into an Argonaute protein, forming RISC.

test.q: Which small RNA class silences transposons in the germline with PIWI proteins?
test.explain: piRNAs partner with PIWI proteins to protect the germline genome from transposons.

test.q: Long noncoding RNAs are defined as longer than ___ nucleotides.
test.explain: The conventional cutoff for lncRNAs is more than 200 nucleotides.

test.q: What is the abbreviation for the process in which double-stranded RNA triggers sequence-specific silencing?
test.explain: RNA interference was discovered by Fire and Mello, who won the 2006 Nobel Prize.

test.q: The nuclear Microprocessor complex consists of DGCR8 and the enzyme ___.
test.explain: Drosha crops the pri-miRNA into a pre-miRNA.

kidTest.q: What does a microRNA do to a recipe RNA?
kidTest.explain: A microRNA grabs a recipe RNA and turns down how much it gets used.

kidTest.q: Is a microRNA big or small?
kidTest.explain: MicroRNAs are tiny pieces of RNA.

kidTest.q: What does the long RNA Xist do?
kidTest.explain: Xist covers an extra X chromosome and makes it go quiet.

kidTest.q: Most RNAs are recipes. What are the special RNAs in this lesson like?
kidTest.explain: Regulatory RNAs help decide which recipes get used.

kidTest.q: Regulatory RNAs are not just messengers. They can act like a b _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: They give orders about which genes are used.

advancedTest.q: A lncRNA knockdown with an ASO causes no effect, but deleting its promoter silences a neighboring gene. The most likely interpretation is:
choices: Transcription or the DNA element, not the RNA, has the effect
The ASO caused strong seed-mediated off-target repression
The lncRNA acts mainly as a sponge for miRNAs
The mature RNA product acts in trans on distant genes
advancedTest.explain: Losing the effect only when the locus is disrupted points to transcription or the DNA element, as with Airn silencing Igf2r.

advancedTest.q: Why do stoichiometric studies doubt most ceRNA claims?
choices: Single transcripts rarely change total site pools enough
Argonaute rapidly degrades sponge transcripts it binds
miRNAs mainly bind targets in the 5' UTR instead
Seed pairing is too weak to bind miRNAs at most sites
advancedTest.explain: Sponging requires a large change in total site abundance, as with CDR1as and its roughly 70 miR-7 sites. Most single transcripts are too scarce to achieve this.

advancedTest.q: Several siRNAs against different genes give the same phenotype and share a 7-nt seed. The best next step is:
choices: Conclude that the genes are in one shared pathway
Test seed-matched controls and siRNA-resistant rescue
Switch to a different transfection lipid reagent
Raise siRNA concentration to strengthen knockdown
advancedTest.explain: A shared seed suggests miRNA-like off-target effects. Seed controls and rescue experiments test whether the phenotype is real.

advancedTest.q: Ribosome profiling of miRNA-repressed targets at steady state best supports which conclusion?
advancedTest.explain: Guo et al. (2010) found that most steady-state repression comes from reduced mRNA levels, through deadenylation-dependent decay.
